summary: Traditional preimplantation genetic testing for in vitro fertilization (IVF) requires invasive trophectoderm biopsy, which may harm the embryo. Non-invasive preimplantation genetic testing (niPGT) utilizing cell-free DNA from spent embryo culture medium (SCM) has been attempted, but trace DNA content, maternal cell contamination and high allele drop-out rates are barriers. Here we report an niPGT methodology achieving high diagnostic accuracy among reportable samples across diverse embryo and disease contexts. Reengineered linear whole-genome amplification (scm-LIANTI) with an extremely low error rate is followed by application of a Bayesian algorithm designed to determine which parental haplotypes are inherited at disease-causing sites. Among 191 SCM samples from 29 families affected by rare monogenic disorders, our method amplified all samples and enabled diagnosis of 220 out of 277 pathogenic alleles. All diagnoses (220/220) were concordant with invasive biopsy control. For select embryos, personalized genome-wide genotyping enabled exploratory polygenic risk assessment for type 2 diabetes. Our methodology requires no modification to IVF workflows and represents a key technological advance towards scalable, accurate and safe niPGT for both monogenic and polygenic diseases. A reengineered linear whole-genome amplification approach combined with Bayesian linkage analysis enables highly accurate non-invasive preimplantation genetic testing of embryos from families with rare monogenic disorders.
title: Highly accurate non-invasive preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic and polygenic diseases from spent medium

summary: The tumour microenvironment (TME) is a multidimensional dynamic and complex system of cells and non-cellular components that not only drives tumour progression but also substantially influences response to therapy. Understanding TME biology for basic research and identifying biomarkers in the TME to stratify patients for therapy is crucial for optimizing therapeutic outcomes. Current standards for investigating TME dynamics, if even considered beyond preclinical work, rely predominantly on samples for tissue staining and sequencing and require invasive procedures to obtain tissue via surgery or biopsies. This leads to limited assessment of spatial heterogeneity and minimal temporal information as this depends on the timing of tissue sampling, which results in undefined clinical utility. Molecular imaging provides promising solutions by enabling non-invasive, real-time multidimensional spatiotemporal probing of the TME that can complement current ex vivo practices. This Review highlights the relevance of molecular imaging agents and methods that can effectively capture spatiotemporal TME characteristics in situ, offering critical insights into tumour behaviour and treatment response. We provide an overview of current preclinical imaging strategies and their applications in identifying cellular and non-cellular components of the TME, along with monitoring progression-associated processes and treatment response. We showcase new developments and avenues being explored in preclinical imaging, as well as offer perspectives into existing and emerging clinical imaging of the TME to enhance patient care and highlight opportunities for improvement. Overall, integrating TME imaging into clinical practice holds the potential to bridge critical gaps in spatiotemporal resolution, ultimately enabling more precise diagnosis, patient stratification and personalized therapeutic interventions. This Review discusses molecular imaging probes and modalities for studying the complexity and dynamics of the tumour microenvironment in preclinical research and further highlights emerging clinical applications in diagnostics and intervention.
title: Advances in molecular imaging of the tumour microenvironment

summary: Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological–environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics. Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia. Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure–function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes. Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research. These findings ground phenotypic–exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions. The generation of individual biophysical digital twins at massive scale from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging enables individualized insights into regional signatures and excitatory/inhibitory balance, with features that can be linked to key phenotypes and expotypes.
title: Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype–expotype architecture of ageing and dementia

summary: While nanomedicines hold great promise for solid tumour therapy, their penetration and access to tumour cells is limited by large glycosylated proteins called mucins that are enriched in the tumour microenvironment. Here we show that mucins induce the disassembly of self-assembled mPEG–polyester micellar nanoparticles into smaller unimers. Leveraging this finding, we designed a mucin-responsive, paclitaxel-conjugated nanomedicine (mrPNM) whose unimers are capable of escaping the mucin-binding barrier. Following intravenous injection, this designer mucin-responsive nanomedicine exhibited markedly deeper penetration than the mucin-nonresponsive nanomedicine and albumin, resulting in 3.9- and 1.5-fold increases in tumour cell delivery, respectively, in a pancreatic mouse tumour model. The mrPNMs also achieved superior tumour growth inhibition compared to both the mucin-nonresponsive nanomedicine and Abraxane, the FDA-approved nanoparticle albumin-bound paclitaxel, in three solid tumour models. The mucin-responsive nanomedicine platform could provide a general strategy for improving the treatment of solid tumours. Tumour-associated mucins induce the disassembly of a designer PEGylated paclitaxel-conjugated nanomedicine into small unimers that escape the mucin-binding barrier, enhancing tumour penetration and therapeutic efficacy in mouse models of solid tumours.
title: Designer mucin-responsive nanomedicine for enhanced solid tumour penetration and therapy

summary: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have shown great potential for disease detection from liquid biopsies. However, the lack of optimized isolation and detection methods limited their clinical application. Here we engineer a bioinspired, reconfigurable, self-powered bubble motor (Butor) microswarm to streamline intelligent isolation and ultrasensitive profiling of circulating EVs for cancer liquid biopsies. Butor microswarm shows jellyfish-like, self-propelled lifting locomotion along lumen-like vertical or inclined tubular path in parallel, allowing rapid isolation (10 min, near 90%) of EV subtypes via three-dimensional directional scanning capture even in high-viscosity biofluids. Furthermore, the buoyancy-activated Butors achieve ultrasensitive EV profiling near a single-particle level, enable early diagnosis of non-small cell lung cancer with an accuracy of up to 94% (95% sensitivity) in a pilot cohort and improve the outcome in cancer staging (I–IV) discrimination, response monitoring of surgical treatment and efficacy prediction of immunotherapy in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. Our self-powered motor represents an intelligent, fast, inexpensive, sensitive and multiplexed liquid biopsy tool for accurate cancer diagnostics and treatment monitoring in clinical settings. A self-powered bubble motor inspired by microswarm motion enables ultrasensitive extracellular vesicles profiling, monitoring of surgical treatment response, staging discrimination, prediction of immunotherapy and early diagnosis in patients with non-small cell lung cancer.
title: Self-powered bubble motor microswarms for ultrasensitive detection, monitoring and prediction in cancer liquid biopsies
